        East Kilbride parents 'defeat all odds' and welcome IVF baby after 17 years of trying

        "We had one shot at this, one chance. And now we have a four-month-old baby sitting here."

        Listen to audio version of this article
        Sponsored by
        0:00 / 4:43
        Instaread
        News
        Rachel Cronin Reporter
        14:22, 24 Nov 2026Updated 07:39, 25 Nov 2026

        A resilient East Kilbride couple have "defeated all odds" by welcoming their first baby by IVF after trying to get pregnant for 17 years. But Sarah and David Ampleford also faced the "worst 11 days of their lives" when their miracle baby Jacob was rushed to Wishaw's NICU with dangerously low blood sugar.

        Wee Jacob, now four months old, was the couple's "one chance" to have a baby, as the only transferrable embryo from their first ever round of IVF treatment last year.

        The pair had been trying to conceive since their marriage in 2009, but faced difficulties due to Sarah's polycystic ovaries.

        ‌

        Glasgow gym to host women’s self-defence course amid 'national emergency' of violence

        Evil Glaswegian child killer could be released under new name in Scotland

        The couple said they repeatedly had no luck and were told by fertility clinics that Sarah should try to lose weight - which is difficult for people with polycystic overies. And after COVID, the mum - now 43 - says she was no longer eligible for IVF on the NHS due to her age.

        Eventually, after a "heartbreaking" situation during a holiday in Portugal where they mistakenly thought Sarah was pregnant, they decided to go private.

        David, 44, told Glasgow Live: "We honestly felt like we had done it, and it didn't happen at that time. It was probably one of the worst heartbreaks we'd had, but it turned into motivation."

        The Amplefords - or "Team Ampie", to their friends - decided to go with private clinic TFP GCRM Fertility Clinic, where Sarah was to undergo a double embryo transfer to increase their chances.

        ‌

        Sarah told Glasgow Live: "We were repeatedly told that the odds were not in our favour, because of my weight and age, and right from the very start we were told that because of those two factors, we would need a double embryo transfer."

        The couple were "ecstatic" when 15 of Sarah's eggs were retrieved, but after five days, the number had dwindled to five. And after the weekend, Sarah and David were left with just one embryo - and "one chance" to get the baby they had wanted since they married 17 years before.

        "We thought, we'll go for it - this is our one and only chance", Sarah added.

        ‌

        Then, almost exactly one year ago, they finally got the results they had been hoping for - though David admits it took a few moments for him to realise the good news, having never seen a positive pregnancy test in all their years of trying.

        Sarah added: "Still to this day, we wake up every single morning and think 'how is this real? How have we got this lucky?'.

        "My dad lives four doors away from us, so we literally took the pregnancy test - covered in pee - straight round to my dad's.

        David added: "That was the only time we've ever tried IVF, we'd never got that far, but we got through against all odds."

        ‌

        However, things became uncertain towards the end of the pregnancy, and Sarah - who had since been diagnosed with gestational diabetes - was taken in for an emergency c-section at just over 39 weeks when Jacob's heart-rate began to drop.

        After he was born on July 23, the couple said an "amazing" nurse named Connie may have saved Jacob's life when she noticed his blood sugar was dangerously low and immediately called the neonatal unit.

        He was whisked away from Sarah's arms and spent 11 days in Wishaw University Hospital's NICU, which the mum said were the "worst 11 days of my life".

        ‌

        Sarah said: "To this day, I think if it wasn't for her, I don't think Jacob would be here. Her quick thinking saved his life."

        She added: "There was a real concern in the back of my mind that 'he might not come out of here'."

        But David added that the nurses at Wishaw Neonatal were "phenomenal".

        ‌

        And after one final night in transitional care, the pair were finally able to welcome Jacob home. And four months later, he is "thriving".

        The new parents hope their story can inspire others looking to try IVF, and having shared their fertility journey on Facebook, they say baby Jacob has become something of a local celeb in East Kilbride.

        David said: "We've met a lot of nice people and we've given them hope. It's amazing to think that our story has helped other people, and to bring other lives into the world.

        "Ten years ago, I would have never believed you if you told me this was my life. So don't give up."

        ‌

        Sarah added: "We are the primary example that it literally takes one egg. We had one shot at this, once chance. And now we have a four-month-old baby sitting here."
